Messages.Author: Malcolm McCallum
Messages.Body:
The much vaunted point system that the opponents of Ian Forrestal are
pointing to should be scrapped as any sort of benchmark, or at least
re-analyzed. Tura Vaughn, for example, has POT, CEL, PRE, and dom.
Brachah has CEL, PRE, and for. If my deck design only uses CEL and PRE
then the two vampires are equally effective save that one is more
expensive. Therefore Tura would be said to be less efficient. Any aspects
of the cards that I do not use in my deck design are completely
irrelevant to that measure of efficiency. The value of any vampire is
completely relative to the deck it is in.

If there were two vampires with the same abilities but one cost twice the
capacity of the other, I would not be surprised to both those vampires in
the same crypt....and I, personally, would not start calling the more
expensive vampire 'broken'. It is simply different. I would use the
bigger one if I wanted to drop an atonement on it, use obedience, minion
tap, galconda, Ancient Influence, Legendary Vampire, absorb damage, blood
doll, or Return to Innocence.

Capacity and Ability need not be related by formula. Rather, abilities
should be given to vampires that would allow for interesting thematic
deck constructions and that reflect the character that the game designers
have imagined.

Muaziz is regarded as under-priced by the point system. Role-playing
wise, I think she is perfectly priced and has just the right abilities.
She strikes terror into the hearts of those who see her come out and she
attracts a lot of fire but it lets Ulugh have a powerful assassin at his
beck and call without forcing the Tremere to load their deck with
obfuscate cards.

I look forward to seeing more vampires with wide-ranging abilities, such
as Ian, so that we'll be able to try new deck ideas. How else will we be
able to see an effective Auspex/Necromancy deck? or
Dominate/Serpentis/Celerity?

How else will we be able to please all those who whine about contesting
vampires becoming a lost aspect of the game?

The solution is to make vampires who are not cost-effective by the old
point system.,...and its a good thing.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
[snip claim that point system should be scrapped/re-analyzed]

> Tura Vaughn, for example, has POT, CEL, PRE, and dom.
> Brachah has CEL, PRE, and for. If my deck design only uses CEL and PRE
> then the two vampires are equally effective save that one is more
> expensive. Therefore Tura would be said to be less efficient. Any aspects
> of the cards that I do not use in my deck design are completely
> irrelevant to that measure of efficiency. The value of any vampire is
> completely relative to the deck it is in.

OK, given. I play with Badger and Camille in my deck, even though I
don't use Potence. Other than that, they are exactly the same vampire,
except that one costs 1 more (which only means that Camille can Atone
and Badger can't...). But I would not want Badger to cost 5. I think
that would be wrong. Just like in Magic (sorry), there shouldn't a 2/2
plain monster for 2G, nor should there be a 2/2 for G, since there is a
fundamental monster which is 2/2 for 1G. The first would suck, and the
second would be too good. That's a benchmark. In Shadowfist, there
shouldn't be a 2 cost 3 fighting plain resource character, nor should
there be a 2 cost 1 fighting plain resource character, since all of the
2 cost no-ability plain resource characters have 2 fighting. That's a
benchmark.

The "point system" is simple to figure out and applies to most
vampires. It is a benchmark. Making vampires with odd or out-of-clan
discipline distributions cheaper would make some vampires too good, as
compared with almost every other vampire in the game. Why should one
vampire be significantly better than all others?

> If there were two vampires with the same abilities but one cost twice the
> capacity of the other, I would not be surprised to both those vampires in
> the same crypt....

Because, since vampires are unique, you need a distribution of different
vampires with the right abilities. Tura and Bracha should not both cost
5, since one is obviously superior to the other. Tura should be (and
is) more expensive.

> and I, personally, would not start calling the more
> expensive vampire 'broken'.

Were Tura a 5, she would be broken.

>It is simply different. I would use the
> bigger one if I wanted to drop an atonement on it, use obedience, minion
> tap, galconda, Ancient Influence, Legendary Vampire, absorb damage, blood
> doll, or Return to Innocence.

Atonement? Only if it's not bigger than 5...

I agree with you in that large vampires have their uses, but consider
your own example. You have 2 slots left to fill in your crypt for your
PRE CEL deck. Your choices are Brachah, Tura and X, who has exactly the
same abilities as Brachah. Who will you put in? As useful as the
things you mention are, you are more likely to put in Brachah and X.
Why do you think so many people play with the "Raven is Camille" rule?

> Capacity and Ability need not be related by formula. Rather, abilities
> should be given to vampires that would allow for interesting thematic
> deck constructions and that reflect the character that the game designers
> have imagined.

Sure, vampires should have neat abilities/detriments. That makes things
interesting. But no vampire should be strictly better than all other
vampires, which Ian clearly is. Note that if he had a higher capacity
(say 9 or 10) I wouldn't be as upset.

> Muaziz is regarded as under-priced by the point system. Role-playing
> wise, I think she is perfectly priced and has just the right abilities.
> She strikes terror into the hearts of those who see her come out and she
> attracts a lot of fire but it lets Ulugh have a powerful assassin at his
> beck and call without forcing the Tremere to load their deck with
> obfuscate cards.

I'll say this again. I don't mean to offend anyone, but I do not play
the Vampire: the Masquerade game. I understand that this card game is
based on that game. But this is not a role-playing game. This is a
card game. Role-playing considerations do not apply to issues of game
balance.

As for Muaziz, you can imagine a 5-point vampire with Muaziz's
disciplines, since this would be exactly comparable with most other 5's
in the game. So you're really paying 2 pool for Muaziz's other
abilities. What if there was a 2-cost master card which increased the
vampire's capacity by 2, made it immune to Blood Hunts, and gave it +1
stealth on all actions? Wouldn't that be very powerful? And Muaziz
starts off with that.

> I look forward to seeing more vampires with wide-ranging abilities, such
> as Ian, so that we'll be able to try new deck ideas. How else will we be
> able to see an effective Auspex/Necromancy deck? or
> Dominate/Serpentis/Celerity?

Playing with master: skill cards, like God intended.

> The solution is to make vampires who are not cost-effective by the old
> point system.,...and its a good thing.

But then older-edition vampires become strictly less powerful than the
new vampires, which is not fair and pisses people off.

James

* James Hamblin *

* je...@cornell.edu *

Messages.Author: James Puzzo
Messages.Body:
Malcolm McCallum (mcca...@pacificcoast.net) wrote:

You will recall that I've already responded to another of your posts, and I
don't have the energy to do a particularly good job here (as if I did there!)
but here goes...

: The much vaunted point system that the opponents of Ian Forrestal are

: pointing to should be scrapped as any sort of benchmark, or at least
: re-analyzed.

That seems to be a fair statement, but a good argument is awaited...

: Tura Vaughn, for example, has POT, CEL, PRE, and dom. Brachah has
: CEL, PRE, and for.

True.

: If my deck design only uses CEL and PRE

: then the two vampires are equally effective save that one is more
: expensive. Therefore Tura would be said to be less efficient.

Would be said to be less efficient TO THAT DESIGN. Now let's say that I want
a deck which uses POT CEL. And then one with POT PRE. And then one with
POT CEL PRE. And then one with POT DOM. Note that Tura can probably fit
into EACH of these deck designs. This makes Tura MORE valuable than Brachah,
does it not? One should have to pay for versatility... and therefore, Tura
should be priced accordingly. Now, if you could care less that a vampire
is versatile, DON'T USE (and don't pay) for the more versatile one. But you
should still have to PAY if you want the versatility. Ian does not effectively
pay for the versatility he provides. By your argument, if I want a POT CEL
deck, I should find the smallest vampires with POT CEL around. And then
when I make a for aus deck, I should find the smallest vamps with those.
And the same goes for any combination of skills... including ones which are
very rare combinations. The fact that Ian may be used in ANY of these deck
designs points to his versatility, something which should be paid for.

: Any aspects of the cards that I do not use in my deck design are

: completely irrelevant to that measure of efficiency. The value of
: any vampire is completely relative to the deck it is in.

A fair statement. But does this mean that I should pay MORE for a weenie
vampire because he/she is pivotal to my deck strategy? Or LESS for an
inner circle member if they are not? The value of any vampire to a given
deck design is variable. The COST for any vampire is fixed based on their
given abilities. You need to weigh the cost with the added value. Asking
for underpriced vampires just makes it easier for you to do less thinking
when building your crypt. I don't see that as making the game any better.

: If there were two vampires with the same abilities but one cost twice the

: capacity of the other, I would not be surprised to both those vampires in

: the same crypt....and I, personally, would not start calling the more
: expensive vampire 'broken'.

That's nice that you wouldn't, but I do not see how it relates to the
discussion of UNDER-pricing. If you wish to use an OVER-priced vampire in
your crypt, that is your weight to bear.

: Capacity and Ability need not be related by formula. Rather, abilities

: should be given to vampires that would allow for interesting thematic
: deck constructions and that reflect the character that the game designers
: have imagined.

So if a game designer were to imagine a little weenie vampire who had the
power to bring about the destruction of the world of darkness as a +1 stealth
undirected action, would that make the design valid simply because they
thought it up? And if you believe that Ian's ability follow the game's
source, why doesn't he pay blood for his use of the arcane to emulate
disciplines he does not have?

: Muaziz is regarded as under-priced by the point system.

And those that feel she is under-priced only have as being under-priced by
1 or 2. Nothing egregious. At least her abilities can be explained as being
a well-trained assassin for Ulugh. How does one explain the free discplines
that Ian gets? His special ability does not seem to honor the source...

: I look forward to seeing more vampires with wide-ranging abilities, such

: as Ian, so that we'll be able to try new deck ideas. How else will we be
: able to see an effective Auspex/Necromancy deck? or
: Dominate/Serpentis/Celerity?

BUT, if you are respecting the game source, it should not be an EASY thing to
use combinations of disciplines which do not occur naturally in the world
of darkness. And it should certainly not be an EASY thing to use a single
vampire in ALL of these combinations without paying for this versatility.
If the cost means nothing, why have it?

: How else will we be able to please all those who whine about contesting

: vampires becoming a lost aspect of the game?

Contestation indicates a values resource. The higher the probability that
something will contest indicates a higher value. By your arguments, Ian is
extremely highly likely to be contested, which should indicate that his
cost is too low. If two Meth's have decided to invest in the same highly
contested resource, they will pay the price. This is, again, a case of
attempting to weigh the benefits with the possible costs. There should be
a BALANCE between expected benefit and cost. If you are HIGHLY contestable,
then this should indicate that the costs are too low for the benefit. If
contestation is HIGHLY unlikely, the benefits probably are overshadowed
by the cost. A _good_ design respects this balance.

: The solution is to make vampires who are not cost-effective by the old

: point system.,...and its a good thing.

I wouldn't mind if the old system were ignored IF (big IF) vampires appeared
to have some semblance of a balance between cost and ability AND a respect
for the source. Ian does not appear to have either. That is the argument.

-spongy

Messages.Author: DOUGDWISE
Messages.Body:
Malcolm,

I think James did a pretty good job of defending the point system as it
stands. There are a couple of things I would like to add though.

I think Ian Forestal is an abusive and unfair vampire that helps the
Tremere to become even more powerful. If the card were printed thus: "Ian
Forestal, 8, THA, AUS, DOM, ani, cel, chi, dem, for, nec, obf, obt, pot,
pre, qui, ser, vis," it might be more obvious at a glance that something
is wrong with it. He has every discipline in the game and all his clan's
basic disciplines are at superior.

In just a run of the mill Tremere deck he would be useful but not overly
powerful. The real degeneracy comes to light when the Tremere start to
add in some disciplines. This guy can fit into any Tremere deck and fit
well. He may not be any better in a particular deck than another Tremere,
but he will be better in all possible Tremere decks than any other
Tremere. No matter what discipline combos are used, the Tremere need
never have to pay more than 8 pool to have them all on a single vampire.
I don't see Ian Forestal being contested as widely as some folks suggest
because he is not going to be useful in many decks other than Tremere
decks. Will the Gangrel want to pay 8 for a vampire with inferior of all
their clan disciplines? Will the Torreador need an 8 capacity vamp with
AUS cel pre even if he has another skill they are trying to incorporate?
Brujah won't want an 8 pot cel pre. His inferior disciplines are not
worth the 8 pool for clans that can't also use his superior disciplines.
Expect to see him in lots of Tremere decks, some Malk decks and only a few
others.

Since you mention Muziz...now there is a design problem vamp. Yes, I'm
sure it is very nice for the Tremere to have a powerful assassin without
having to load their deck with obfuscate cards. Of course, if any other
non-obf and non-pro clan wants to have that ability they do have to load
those obfuscate cards in the old card mix. The way it stands now, the
Tremere get to use stealth without worrying about the cards coming up or
diluting their focus. Soon, they will be able to use every discipline
without worrying about how to make it work in the crypt. Truly they are
the chosen ones. ;-)

I've said it before and I'll say it again: There is apparently some kind
of bias toward the Tremere in the design process. I am not the only one
who thinks so. It seems as if the only folks on the group who support
this are the Tremere fans within the game. Go figure. ;-)

Good luck with the Tremere decks,
Doug Dunaway

Messages.Body:
DOUGDWISE (doug...@aol.com) wrote:
: I think Ian Forestal is an abusive and unfair vampire that helps the

: Forestal, 8, THA, AUS, DOM, ani, cel, chi, dem, for, nec, obf, obt, pot,
: pre, qui, ser, vis," it might be more obvious at a glance that something
: is wrong with it. He has every discipline in the game and all his clan's
: basic disciplines are at superior.

As I've mentioned before, they obviously didn't want to print the disciplines
on the card because then Ian wouldn't be able to use any of the cute new
disciplines which could possibly be added as time goes on. Not only is Ian
overpowered now, but he will GROW in power as time goes on.

: In just a run of the mill Tremere deck he would be useful but not overly
: powerful. The real degeneracy comes to light when the Tremere start to
: add in some disciplines.

Or when previously unworkable combinations of skills are now possible, given
any clan. Many folks are not afraid of discipline masters... and at most
three can give Ian superior in any three that you like. Quite cute.

: but he will be better in all possible Tremere decks than any other
: Tremere.

Which should indicate his value (underpriced).

: I don't see Ian Forestal being contested as widely as some folks suggest

: because he is not going to be useful in many decks other than Tremere
: decks.

If you already play with discipline masters, than you won't mind tossing Ian
into just about any deck.

: Will the Gangrel want to pay 8 for a vampire with inferior of all
: their clan disciplines?

They will if they'd like to add some auspex. Or to contest Tremere unique
locations in a hoser capacity. Who knows? The addition of a do-it-all
vampire makes previously unworkable strategies workable. Maybe there really
is a viable reason why the Gangrel could use him.

: Will the Torreador need an 8 capacity vamp with AUS cel pre even if

: he has another skill they are trying to incorporate?

Perhaps not, but if they wanted to incorporate another clan for odd
combinations, Ian is someone who can bridge that gap.

: Brujah won't want an 8 pot cel pre. His inferior disciplines are not

: worth the 8 pool for clans that can't also use his superior disciplines.

That's just fine... but he also sets a precedent for future cross disciplined
vampires. His value should not depend on whether he will work in a given
deck strategy. His value should be based on the inherent versatility and
usability of his abilities.

-spongy

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 23 Aug 1996, Malcolm McCallum wrote:

> The much vaunted point system that the opponents of Ian Forrestal are
> pointing to should be scrapped as any sort of benchmark, or at least
> re-analyzed.

[snip]

> Any aspects
> of the cards that I do not use in my deck design are completely
> irrelevant to that measure of efficiency. The value of any vampire is
> completely relative to the deck it is in.

Not true. The value of the vampire is the abilitiy of it to be put into
any deck. The value of the vampire _to_that_deck_ is quite different
than the value of a vampire in particular. Otherwise, my payment for
vampires in my mono-discipline decks should be extremely cheap indeed.

> If there were two vampires with the same abilities but one cost twice the
> capacity of the other, I would not be surprised to both those vampires in
> the same crypt....and I, personally, would not start calling the more

> expensive vampire 'broken'. It is simply different. I would use the

> bigger one if I wanted to drop an atonement on it, use obedience, minion
> tap, galconda, Ancient Influence, Legendary Vampire, absorb damage, blood
> doll, or Return to Innocence.

No one is calling the bigger vampire broken. What we are saying is this:

Arika wouldn't be too cheap if she were only 8 (or 9) capacity, would she?
Why should she pay for here out-of-clan disciplines? They aren't
likely to be used. In my presence-only deck, shouldn't I only have to
pay 6 (2 for discipline, 4 for special ability)?

Aren't the above statements ludicrous? They are the statements being
made by the design team and Shawn regarding Ian Forestal.

> Muaziz is regarded as under-priced by the point system.

True.

>Role-playing
> wise, I think she is perfectly priced and has just the right abilities.
> She strikes terror into the hearts of those who see her come out and she
> attracts a lot of fire but it lets Ulugh have a powerful assassin at his

> beck and call without forcing the Tremere to load their deck with
> obfuscate cards.

Just because a vampire inspires terror means nothing. Camille can
inspire terror, but at least she costs the right amount. Muaziz, on the
other hand, is too cheap.

> I look forward to seeing more vampires with wide-ranging abilities, such
> as Ian, so that we'll be able to try new deck ideas. How else will we be
> able to see an effective Auspex/Necromancy deck? or
> Dominate/Serpentis/Celerity?

With Master skill cards. With vampires who have these disciplines. With
Ian (if his cost were appropriate).

> How else will we be able to please all those who whine about contesting
> vampires becoming a lost aspect of the game?

> The solution is to make vampires who are not cost-effective by the old
> point system.,...and its a good thing.

Why? So that all the old (balanced) cards become obsolete. If you truly
believe this, I am sorry.

No, this is not what I am saying, and I would appreciate if you would
stop putting words in my mouth, thank you. My original comment was on
discipline costs, and how I personally felt that at higher levels, they
may be overpriced. This is WotC's "design point" system, and not the
one described on the net. I asked for people's input because I wanted
to hear what they had to say.

As a side note, I am starting to believe that this Ian Forestal
discussion is giving me gas.

What I state as my opinion is now being reworked into discussions of
other cards. I *never* said word one about Arika, lower cost or not.
My input was on the workings of the design behind Ian, most of which
have been ripped apart as heresy and reworded for further critical
analysis which I have not lent my input to. Now I fully expect to see
all my previous posts assimilated together into another lambaste on Ian
and the design team. I can't wait--whee.

It all comes down to personal opinion, and some opinions will always
differ than the others. I'm sorry some people don't care for how the
design/development team of WotC does things, but being a part of it, all
I can say is that we strive to become better each day. If it is not to
someone's liking, then all I can do is apologize and try to incorporate
changes to make it better. I cannot, however, cater tastes when the
differing opinions of the DT themselves must come into swing. I am but
a single part.

Alright, Shawn. Take a deep breath. Exhale. Try to relax.

This Ian Forestal thing has all of us rather worked up. The Corrupter is
just the person who had his post phrased in a way which made it sound like he
was putting words in your mouth(from your perspective, I can see that it
would seem like he was). I'm not trying to necessarily excuse him here(not
that I have the right to judge him or you in the first place), but as a way
of explaining what and why he said:

a) You haven't been on the group for a while; I think since you made your
statement about out-of-clan disciplines being cheaper than the usual costs
which we posted as our basis for the "point system". The fact that you
haven't responded to our attempted rebuttals, or been able to, just makes us
frustrated, especially when newbies who don't have as much background in the
game as us or you start saying things like "The point system ought to be
scrapped; Tura vaughn should only cost as much as Brachah for a
Presence/Celerity deck."

"point system" we refer to works; a number of us explained, and since Ian was
riding on our minds, and since you had been unable to respond, our debating
frustrations and desire to make our points came out on those posts, as we
used Ian as an example of a card which to US violates the point system. The
Corrupter's quoted text was basically a rhetorical device, intended to make a
point about the point system and game balance, not necessarily a personal
attack(knowing the Corrupter, I wouldn't take it that way).

>As a side note, I am starting to believe that this Ian Forestal
>discussion is giving me gas.

Hey, me too... I think that the reasons are slightly different, though. ;)

>What I state as my opinion is now being reworked into discussions of

>My input was on the workings of the design behind Ian, most of which

>all my previous posts assimilated together into another lambaste on Ian
>and the design team. I can't wait--whee.

We don't lambast.(At least, not most of us.) What we try to do is debate.
Point. By Point. By Point. Sometimes we expect people to know every
argument back to the start of the thread. I'm sorry if our style of
discussion makes you uncomfortable, or even angry at us, Shawn. That is not
it's intent in any way. I believe that I can speak for most of the group
here in saying that what we want is an open discussion of design and balance
issues, and your participation in such a discussion would be valued and even
needed so that we don't end up just talking to ourselves and coming to a
general consensus which nonetheless will have no effect on the design team or
WotC's policies in any way. I know that your time is limited. But do you
think that we could have a discussion about the principles of game balance,
especially as they relate to Jyhad, with your input?

>It all comes down to personal opinion, and some opinions will always
>differ than the others.

Well, there are arguments too... Logic and all that. Of course, what is
logical and illogical will generally come down to opinion as well. I don't
suppose that if you want to discuss these issues with us, you'd be willing to
either have us define the format, or come to some agreement (I haven't seen
the newsgroup charter yet... :( ).

>I'm sorry some people don't care for how the
>design/development team of WotC does things, but being a part of it, all
>I can say is that we strive to become better each day. If it is not to

>differing opinions of the DT themselves must come into swing. I am but

letting them see our posts for themselves? I don't suppose that any of the

and maybe post? The ability to talk to more people from WotC would enable us
to communicate our concerns to you better, and perhaps make Jyhad/V:teS a
better game in the long run.

An Ivory Tower idea assumes a unified front. On the contrary, we are far

Value is far different than cost. While a card might not be valuable to a
certain deck, that doesn't mean its cost for _any_ particular deck should
be lower.

To address your idea to drop the point system, I have one question:
Do you want to make the original Jyhad set obselete?

All of the old vampires were created with some version of the point system
(how accurate our idea of what exactly that is is debatable). If the
design team starts making new vampires willy-nilly without the point
system, those new vampires that cost too much will find themselves almost
never used. Those new vampires that cost too little will find themselves
used more often. In the end, you get to a point where the old vampires
are all totally outclassed by the new ones, with the only way to compete
being to play _only_ the new cards. Smart idea.

objective way to tell if something is too powerful/weak, other than "Looks
kinda Okay to me, Jed. How 'bout you?" "Dunno, about right, maybe..."

Again, an undercosted card doesn't necessarily break a game. Blythe

> that a deck that derives its strength from Ian has a weak link.

Would my all-presence deck which has Arika (cost 7 instead of 11) have a
"weak link" because of her inclusion? It would derive its strength
from her (even though it is still happy to include her as an 11). I mean,
I only plan on _using_ presence. Why should I pay for the others?

> That said, I cringe at the way that Summon the Serpent will almost ensure
> Ian's arrival in any game where he is really necessary.

Actually, you couldn't do that to Ian. He doesn't have Serpentis, he just
can play as if he had it. (Wow! The first time it actually makes a
difference... This and Kiss of Ra)

> Malcolm McCallum, Unconcerned Gamer?

Would you be unconcerned if Arika cost 9? After all, how many decks _use_
6 disciplines anyway?

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Malcolm McCallum wrote:
>
> We say that the value of a vampire is completely relative to the deck it
> is in and less so to the decks it is opposed to. Capacity should NOT be
> considered the value of a vampire nor should there be a direct
> link/formulaic relationship between capacity and abilities.

Well, it is natural to equate cost = value. With most of the Jyhad
original set vampires as a standard (Anvil notwithstanding), every
vampire who is printed can and should be compared to existing vampires.

It turns out that the "point system" as we have defined it conforms
rather well to those vampires. Why should we not compare all vampires
in this system and conclude "this one is too cheap" or "this one is too
expensive"?

> Big vamps
> should have more abilities than small ones. Beyond that, whatever the
> team comes up with will likely (Yes, I trust them) be a fair creature.

But even with that statement you admit to the basis of the point
system. Big vamps should have more abilities than small ones. Well,
how many should small ones have? You certainly would want a 2 capacity
vampire with a superior, would you?

Were WotC to print such a vampire, the game would become unbalanced.
Why should small vampires have so many abilities. How come X new
vampire is a 2 with superior Fortitude, but Giuliano Vincenzi is a 2
with inferior fortitude?

> Our group would have been quite happy to play with the unerrated Blythe.
> We know that there are enough variable factors in the game to prevent the
> super weenie from becoming a dominant or even noticeable factor.

But even with eratta, Blythe is over powered. Compare her to Ricky van
Demsy. They are both 3's. Ricky has 2 inferiors. UEBlythe has two
superiors, and -1 hand damage against Malks. OK. What if they printed
NewRicky, a 3 point Gangrel with FOR PRO and -1 hand damage against
Malkavians. Which is the better vampire? Obviously, this new one,
since (especially for Tremere) clan-specific disadvantages are nowhere
near as bad as regular disadvantages. If NewRicky had simply -1 hand
damage, it would much harder to determine which was the better vamp.

> The 'point system' is a shaky axiom used by some. Back up and try the
> logical arguments without it. There is no question that Ian does not fit
> the system yet he still may be a valid vampire. That would invalidate the
> 'system'.

The argument above does not use the point system. It just compares
vampires and attempts to determine which vampires are better than
others.

Also, vampires don't _have_ to conform to the point system. Simply
because so many of them do is reason enough to say that certain vampires
(Muaziz, Blythe, Ian, etc.) (Look at that... they're all Tremere...) are
overpowered.

> Have faith
> that a deck that derives its strength from Ian has a weak link.

The point is not that Ian will break the game. Uniqueness of vampires
prevents him from doing so. However, more vampires printed according to
this trend might break the game.

You cannot deny that the point system conforms to most existing
vampires. That said, why should we not use it as a benchmark? If
Sabbat comes out and all/most of those vampires go against this system,
then we will have to revise it.

James

When I first heard about the so-called "point system" I was rather happy
knowing that there are some checks-and-balances built into the
design system. This way certain vampires won't become "must haves" while
others become wallpaper. I got into V:TES because I became disenchanted
with the whole "this deck kicks butt, but it cost a hellacious amount of
money to build" thing, currently inherent in Magic. I still play Magic,
but I enjoy V:TES more, partially because I have a chance to compete with a
limited budget and card set.

Now I may just be naive, but I like to believe that a point system for
building vampires is a good idea. I mean, why should I pay 5 pool to bring
out a vamp with a certain skill set when I can pay 4 for the exact same
vampire, unless I want the vamp to be a little bigger from the start? I'm
not saying that this is the case with Ian, but if you don't hold to some
sort of point system then you make some vampires inherently better than
others simply because they do more for less. Ian is definately a "bargain"
vampire.

Just my .02.

Messages.Author: DOUGDWISE
Messages.Body:
Greetings to All,

On this subject of point systems for designing vampires I have to come
down in favor of one. I recall a game called Spellfire (anybody remember
that?) that had something called creatures or heroes, I can't remember
much about it, and they were just put in the deck and brought out when you
needed them to do battle. They ranged in power from 10 (high) to 1 and
the 10s cost no more to bring into play than the ones. Nobody that I ever
spoke with who played or saw the game could ever understand why someone
would play with anything except their highest power cards since they all
cost the same.
I'm sorry if I am getting some of the details wrong but the concept was as
I state. I just don't recall much about the game and that sort of helps
make the point. The way they did the creature cards for Spellfire was
stupid because there was no reason to ever use anything but a big monster
of a ten. Why did they even print the ones? They had no "Point System",
no way of appropriately costing the cards so that there would be some
thought required to build a deck. One of the great things about Jyhad was
it's mix of clans and disciplines and trying to get that right mix of
vampires and library cards. Not every clan had inherent stealth or damage
prevention so it was necessary to choose carefully and to blend the
vampires in the crypt to get them to work. Without apprpriate costing,
crypt building would be on the Spellfire plan: "OK, let's just put all of
the vampires with the most disciplines and abilities in 'cause they all
cost the same." This seems to be a "dumbing down" of the strategy levels
and the challenge level of the game and so I would oppose Ian Forestal as
advertised for this reason alone.
Let's _not_ forget the point system. Shawn may never share with us the
system that the design team uses (used?) for vampires but it seems obvious
that there was one. We need it to keep this game interesting. Do we
really want a 3-capacity PRE OBF Prince or a 5-capacity POT PRO FOR CEL
that can attack any minion at +1 stealth? >shiver<
Keep up the debate. Who knows, somebody may actually form a new opinion.
Doug Dunaway

Messages.Author: Malcolm McCallum
Messages.Body:
The most common point that people seem to make in favour of the point
system is that without it we will get horrendously abusive cards (they
then proceed to describe obscene card ideas). Let's dismiss this idea
immediately. When I advocate abandoning a point system, I do not advocate
going mad. I suggest that the design team should be able to push at the
edges of the envelope a little and give us more variety. A vampire who,
by the point system, has more abilities than he should for his age is not
unfair for anyone. Everyone has equal access to that vampire (generally).
Yes, by being more efficient than some, it will take the wind out of the
sails of some of our old stand-by vampires. On the other hand, most
crypts contain a few (majority) vampires who are not making the grade
anyway. There will be filler.

In the game environment that I play in, capacity is often more useful
than the abilities that the vampires come with. An Inner Council Member
does not rear its head without being Minion Tapped within the first few
turns. That vampire was played to make the minion tap more
efficient/valuable. The fact that the 11 pointer also has 4 votes and
everything necessary in superior is a plus. When a Galconda is dropped on
it the next turn for another 11 the value by the point system is even
more moot.

A 1 capacity vampire can drop a Princely title upon itself fairly easily
in the opening moves. How then can we put a concrete value on a vampire
that relates a title to capacity to abilities? It is an artificial
assignment.

As I understand it, the point system is not something that the design
team has declared it used. Rather, it is a pattern that was detected and
'decoded' by players. There is some disagreement on which abilities are
worth what capacity because the de-ciphered system is not wholly
consistent with the vampires that existed (very nearly though). This
might mean that the design team simply managed to create an apparently
balanced collection of vampires in the first run. It does not mean that
they are bound by that. It would mean though that they are likely
concious of some rudimentary game-design philosophies and will likely,
based on previous experience and expertise, continue to produce a fairly
balanced system.

You see signs of escalation. I too see it. I also see signs of
under-powering. There were some damnably useless cards in that last
expansion. Of course, there were some damnably useless cards in the basic
Jyhad as well, non? As well, there were some obscenely overpowered ones.
Misdirection anyone?

Seek moderation in all things.

Frankly, I dread the Sabbat expansion. I have this horrible feeling that
it will wonk the game. I had the feeling before Ian and have it still
regardless of him. I think it is simply a general fear of losing
something that works. On the other hand, I'm going to try to keep my
faith in the design team. Vampire has always been the game that was
Magic's opposite. The more Magic messes itself up, the more likely we are
to get a better game out of the Vampire expansions.

Messages.Author: theCorrupter
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 20 Sep 1996, Malcolm McCallum wrote:

> The most common point that people seem to make in favour of the point
> system is that without it we will get horrendously abusive cards (they
> then proceed to describe obscene card ideas).

Like:
Blythe Candaleria -- TRE 3 AUS THA -- -1 hand damage vs. MAL

A small card, highly overpowered for its cost.

> Let's dismiss this idea
> immediately. When I advocate abandoning a point system, I do not advocate
> going mad.

What do you advocate then? Let's read on...

>I suggest that the design team should be able to push at the
> edges of the envelope a little and give us more variety.

I see. Rather than having an objective standard, you propose the design
team just make some vampires and if they look "about right, more or less"
its okay?

> A vampire who,
> by the point system, has more abilities than he should for his age is not
> unfair for anyone.

So if I want to make a standard Gangrel disciplined deck, and an
overpowered Toreador is made, I should throw it in or abandon my Gangrel?
It _is_ unfair that Toreador, for example, would be able to get bargains
that the Gangrel don't.

If your answer is to make underpriced vampires for everyone, then I have
to violently object. Planned obselesence for cards in a balanced game is
a bad idea.

> Everyone has equal access to that vampire (generally).
> Yes, by being more efficient than some, it will take the wind out of the
> sails of some of our old stand-by vampires. On the other hand, most
> crypts contain a few (majority) vampires who are not making the grade
> anyway. There will be filler.

So, this New Order you propose will cause creation of cards that are "just
a bit under/over-priced, make old vampires less useful, and all be
justified by "most ... are not making the grade anyway"? Malcolm, I'm
sorry, but I can't see how you can prefer this haphazard,
cross-our-fingers-and-hope philosophy of design over a balanced standard.

> In the game environment that I play in, capacity is often more useful
> than the abilities that the vampires come with. An Inner Council Member
> does not rear its head without being Minion Tapped within the first few
> turns. That vampire was played to make the minion tap more
> efficient/valuable.

However, you lost not only pool in bringing it out, you lost influence
time. The minion tap can't give you back that time you spent. Thus, if
that tapped IC member gets Rushed into oblivion, you have lost :
1) Pool not reclaimed by the tap
2) A Master phase (minion tap)
3) several influences
4) opporunities to do other things

> The fact that the 11 pointer also has 4 votes and
> everything necessary in superior is a plus. When a Galconda is dropped on
> it the next turn for another 11 the value by the point system is even
> more moot.

How so? No offense, Malcolm, but if your analysis of the situation
brings you to that conclusion, you do not understand game theory enough to
be arguing to remove the point system.

> A 1 capacity vampire can drop a Princely title upon itself fairly easily
> in the opening moves. How then can we put a concrete value on a vampire
> that relates a title to capacity to abilities? It is an artificial
> assignment.

All assignments in the game are artificial. However, that doesn't mean
they should be inconsistent.

> As I understand it, the point system is not something that the design
> team has declared it used. Rather, it is a pattern that was detected and
> 'decoded' by players. There is some disagreement on which abilities are
> worth what capacity because the de-ciphered system is not wholly
> consistent with the vampires that existed (very nearly though). This
> might mean that the design team simply managed to create an apparently
> balanced collection of vampires in the first run. It does not mean that
> they are bound by that. It would mean though that they are likely
> concious of some rudimentary game-design philosophies and will likely,
> based on previous experience and expertise, continue to produce a fairly
> balanced system.

Compare the original set to Dark Sovereigns if you believe that.

> You see signs of escalation. I too see it. I also see signs of
> under-powering. There were some damnably useless cards in that last
> expansion. Of course, there were some damnably useless cards in the basic
> Jyhad as well, non? As well, there were some obscenely overpowered ones.
> Misdirection anyone?

Misdirection is not overpowered for several reasons:
Wake with Evening's Freshness, Rat's Warning, and 2nd Tradition

The fact that these cards could totally nullify the pool cost add a _huge_
threat to using it. (X pool for virtually no effect).

But, to address this whole issue:

If the original Jyhad set fell into this range

xxx x x xx x x x xx x x
Useless--------------------------------------------------------Overpowered

with cards being of varying degrees of usefulness, that does not mean that
the following (more of Useless, more Overpowered) is good, just because
the average is the same.

x x xxx xx x x x x xx xxxxxc xx x
Useless--------------------------------------------------------Overpowered

> Frankly, I dread the Sabbat expansion. I have this horrible feeling that
> it will wonk the game. I had the feeling before Ian and have it still
> regardless of him. I think it is simply a general fear of losing
> something that works. On the other hand, I'm going to try to keep my
> faith in the design team. Vampire has always been the game that was
> Magic's opposite. The more Magic messes itself up, the more likely we are
> to get a better game out of the Vampire expansions.

I too fear the Sabbat expansion. Given Shawn's reaction to our comments
on Ian, a playtester friend's warning that there were "bigger fish to
fry", the seeming escalation of recent WotC products in general, I am
afraid. Most of my playgroup is looking forward with apprehension, and
more than half of us have decided that if Sabbat is as we fear it may be,
we will likely be done with the game.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Malcom McCallum wrote:
"The difference is that Corrupter and Co. have
immersed themselves into an ivory tower of netizens. The 'point system'
should be scrapped. I stand by that"

I fail to see how advocating game balance is immersing ones self in an
ivory tower. The "Point System" as it were is not something that can be
scrapped, as it is the theoretical system that was used to build the bulk
of the vampires in the game, i.e. the vamps from the basic set. The
system that was used to create all the basic vampires (wheither it is the
player surmised "point system" or not) created a bench mark by which all
other vampires in the game are judged. This is not debateable, it is
simply the case. What ever system was used to create the basic vampires
is quantifiable, and is one of the base balancing factors in the game.

Without this balancing factor, there would be no logic to the vampires in
the game, and the vampires would be unbalanced. If KoKo had POT while
Lupo had pot, yet they were both still 2 point vampires, that would be
unfair, regardless of the "story" ideas behind it. As it is, for the most
part, most vampires are balanced with eachother, and thus the game works.

Without the balance of the "point system" there is no stick to measure the
worth of a vampire by. Regardless of wheither or not you belive in the
"point system", Nakova is too expensive for what you get, while Anvil is
too cheap. These are universally accepted truths, and this is because of
what they get in comparrison to other similar cost vampires. The "point
system" can easily be ignored as a concept, but you cannot ignore the
comparison of equally priced vampires.

Balance in card games is a very teniuous thing, and messing around with
that ballance tends to screw things up quite a bit. Granted, Ian will not
destroy the game by himself, and neither will Muaziz or Blythe, but the
more "wrong" cards are printed, the further the game will suffer.

Arbitrary atributes and abilities work just fine in a Role Playing Game.
In the sticky ballance that is a card game, it just will not do.

He then wrote:
"Our group would have been quite happy to play with the unerrated Blythe."

But then what possible use would Dr. John Cassey Cassem have? He would be
then completely obsolete, as opposed to just somewhat obsolete, as he is
now.

And finally, he wrote:
"In the game environment that I play in, capacity is often more useful
than the abilities that the vampires come with. An Inner Council Member
does not rear its head without being Minion Tapped within the first few
turns. That vampire was played to make the minion tap more
efficient/valuable."

And in our enviornment, any IC member who is minion tapped for any
worthwhile ammount of blood is rushed, mangled, and burned before they can
even hunt. Everything is relative.
